market_context: United States/general English; cooked cuts compared skinless or trimmed of separable fat and without added oil
title: Leanest meats: a ranking of lower-fat cuts

seo.title: Leanest meat cuts: fat, protein, and calories ranked
seo.meta_description: Skinless turkey and chicken breast, pork tenderloin, and trimmed beef round can provide substantial protein with roughly 2–8 g fat per 100 g cooked.
seo.search_intent: Identify genuinely lean meat cuts and compare fat, protein and calories under comparable cooked conditions.

excerpt: “Lean meat” depends more on the cut than the animal. Skinless turkey breast can fall around 1–3 grams fat per 100 grams cooked, chicken breast 3–4 grams, pork tenderloin 3–5 grams, and very lean beef round roughly 5–8 grams.
content_html:
There is no single lean animal and single fatty animal. Cut, skin, separable fat, and cooking method can change the result more than the species name. A useful comparison uses cooked meat without skin or visible separable fat and without added oil.

Practical ranking per 100 g cooked

CutFatProteinCalories
Skinless turkey breast~1–3 g~29–30 g~135–150
Skinless chicken breast~3–4 g~30–31 g~160–170
Trimmed pork tenderloin~3–5 g~26–28 g~150–170
Very lean beef eye of round/round~5–8 g~28–30 g~180–210
Lean pork loin~6–9 g~27–30 g~180–210

The ranges reflect real variation among entries. A steak with visible edge fat is not equivalent to the same named cut trimmed to lean only.

Turkey and chicken stand out when skin is removed

Skinless turkey breast can land around 1–3 g fat/100 g and chicken breast around 3–4 g while both provide roughly 29–31 g protein. A turkey entry at 2 g and chicken at 3.6 g differ by only 1.6 g fat per 100 g.

Pork can be as lean as some poultry

Well-trimmed cooked pork tenderloin can fall around 3–5 g fat/100 g, overlapping skinless chicken breast in many data entries. Pork belly or fatty shoulder, by contrast, can exceed 20–50 g fat/100 g depending on the product.

Beef varies enormously by cut

A trimmed beef round cut can land around 5–8 g fat/100 g cooked with 28–30 g protein. A well-marbled ribeye can exceed 20 g fat. That can mean more than 12 g extra fat and roughly 110 additional calories per 100 g.

Ground meat needs its percentage

Ground meat labeled 90% lean is not equivalent to 95% or 80% lean. A 10-percentage-point difference represents 10 g fat per 100 g raw product before cooking losses. The lean percentage is more informative than simply “beef” or “turkey.”

Pan oil can exceed the natural difference between cuts

Ten grams of oil adds 10 g fat and about 90 calories. That is more added fat than the entire difference between turkey breast and a trimmed beef round serving in the table.

The useful takeaway

Common very lean choices include skinless turkey breast, skinless chicken breast, pork tenderloin, and well-trimmed beef round. Exact order varies by entry, but the rule is stable: compare the cut, skin, separable fat and added cooking fat—not just the animal.

faq.question: What is the leanest common meat?
faq.answer: Skinless turkey breast is often among the lowest-fat cooked cuts, around 1–3 g fat per 100 g.

faq.question: Can pork be lean?
faq.answer: Yes. Well-trimmed pork tenderloin can be roughly 3–5 g fat/100 g cooked, overlapping some poultry cuts.

faq.question: Is beef always high in fat?
faq.answer: No. Trimmed beef round can be around 5–8 g fat/100 g, while heavily marbled cuts can exceed 20 g.
